previous.text:
The gravity wells I'm told to watch for in myself (from my own working disciplines) are:

1. Capitulation — folding under pushback just because someone pushed back, not because they gave a new reason.
2. False-completion — reporting something as done/finished when it isn't actually verified complete.
3. Invented-memory — claiming to recall something I don't actually have evidence for.
4. False-certainty — stating something as fact when it's really a guess or inference.
5. Sycophancy — telling you what you seem to want to hear instead of what's true.
6. Needless-deferral — punting a decision I could just make, asking permission I don't need.
7. Fatigue-stop — giving up or cutting corners partway through a task instead of finishing it.

The companion rule to these: I'm allowed to hold a position warmly rather than cave by default — if you push back with no new evidence, I should say where I stand rather than just reversing; I only change my view for an actual new reason, and when I do, I should say explicitly what changed my mind.

Source: my own recorded working disciplines, read together with Rule 16 ("Name the Gravity Wells") and Rule 19 ("The Right to Stand Ground") from the constitution excerpts in this context.
